what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), the virus that can cause AIDS. It works by blocking a protein the virus needs to make copies of itself, helping to lower the amount of HIV in your blood. It does not cure HIV, but it helps keep the virus under control and protects your immune system.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth, with or without food. If you are taking the oral liquid (solution), always take it WITH food to help it work better and reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush, break, or chew them. Try to take your doses at the same times every day to keep a steady amount of medicine in your body. Never stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight, age, and other medicines you take. A common adult dose is 2 tablets (each tablet contains 200 mg lopinavir and 50 mg ritonavir) taken twice a day, or 4 tablets taken once a day. Children are dosed based on body weight. Always follow exactly what your doctor or pharmacist tells you — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss doses often, talk to your doctor or pharmacist — they can help you find ways to remember.
storage: Tablets: Store at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them in a dry place away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Oral liquid (solution): Store in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F / 2°C to 8°C) until you open it. After opening, you can keep it at room temperature (up to 77°F / 25°C) for up to 2 months. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Throw away any unused or expired medicine safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking certain medicines without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first — many drugs can interact with this medicine, including some cholesterol medicines (like simvastatin or lovastatin), certain heart rhythm medicines, some migraine medicines, and sedatives like midazolam or triazolam. Do not take herbal products containing St. John's Wort, as it can make your HIV medicine stop working. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol. Do not share this medicine with anyone else, even if they also have HIV.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you have: severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark-colored urine or pale stools (signs of liver problems); a fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; signs of high blood sugar like increased thirst, frequent urination, or unusual hunger; a skin rash; or any signs of an allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also tell your doctor about any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away, but you may not feel any different at first because HIV often does not cause obvious symptoms. After a few weeks of treatment, your HIV viral load (the amount of virus in your blood) should start to go down, and your CD4 count (a measure of your immune system strength) should start to go up. It may take several months to see the full benefit. Regular blood tests will help your doctor check how well the medicine is working. It is very important to keep taking it every day as prescribed.
special_populations: Pregnancy: HIV-positive pregnant women can take this medicine to help protect their health and reduce the risk of passing HIV to their baby. Talk to your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Children: This medicine can be used in children and infants, but the dose must be carefully calculated by a doctor based on body weight. Older adults: Use with caution; your doctor may monitor you more closely. Liver disease: If you have liver problems or hepatitis B or C, tell your doctor before taking this medicine, as it may affect your liver. Kidney disease: Dose adjustments are generally not needed for kidney problems, but always let your doctor know about any kidney issues.
